questions.q: What is the state after applying H to qubit 1 of |00⟩, before any CNOT is applied?
options: (|00⟩ + |10⟩)/√2 — a separable state, not yet entangled
questions.explain: H on qubit 1 alone puts only qubit 1 in superposition; qubit 2 stays definitely |0⟩. The computed vector is [0.7071, 0, 0.7071, 0], which is still a product state (H|0⟩)⊗|0⟩.

questions.q: After applying CNOT (control=q1, target=q2) to (|00⟩+|10⟩)/√2, what state results?
questions.explain: The |10⟩ term has control=1, so its target flips to give |11⟩; the |00⟩ term's control=0 leaves it untouched. The result is the Bell state (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2.

options: Matching coefficients forces a contradiction: ad=0 and bd=1/√2 can't both hold alongside ac=1/√2 and bc=0 for any a,b,c,d
Because the state has an odd number of terms
Because tensor products can only be formed from basis states, never superpositions
It actually can be written that way — the state is separable
questions.explain: Setting the product's coefficients (ac, ad, bc, bd) equal to (1/√2, 0, 0, 1/√2) leads to a direct contradiction, proving no single-qubit factorization exists — the formal definition of entanglement.

questions.q: What do the measurement probabilities of (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 reveal?
options: 0.5 probability each for |00⟩ and |11⟩, and exactly 0 for the mixed outcomes |01⟩ and |10⟩ — perfect correlation
Equal 0.25 probability for all four outcomes
questions.explain: Squaring the amplitudes [0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071] gives [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5] — the two qubits always agree when measured, which a separable (unentangled) state could not guarantee.

questions.q: Starting from |01⟩ instead of |00⟩, then applying H to qubit 1 and the same CNOT, which Bell state results?
questions.explain: H on qubit 1 of |01⟩ gives (|01⟩+|11⟩)/√2; applying CNOT flips the target on the |11⟩ term (control=1) to give |10⟩, leaving |01⟩ untouched, so the result is (|01⟩+|10⟩)/√2 — confirmed by direct computation.
